Performance and Efficiency Trade-offs in Deep Learning Architectures for Sugarcane Disease DetectionFaraz AhmedDepartment of Computer ScienceChrist Deemed to be UniversityBangalore, INDIAxav3170@gmail.comVaruna GuptaDepartment of Computer Science Christ Deemed to be UniversityBangalore, INDIAvarunagupta.cs@gmail.comKamal UpretiDepartment of Computer Science Christ Deemed to be UniversityBangalore, INDIAkamalupreti1989@gmail.comAbstract— Early and accurate detection of sugarcane leaf diseases is crucial for enhancing the productivity of crop and precision agriculture. This research compares the performance of six deep learning architectures namely Custom CNN, VGG16, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3 and EfficientNet-B0 for multiclass classification of sugarcane leaf diseases. All models were trained in a common experimental framework, including five architectures that were trained using transfer learning with the ImageNet dataset, and a Custom CNN that was trained from scratch. The results were evaluated using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, confusion matrices and computational efficiency metrics such as the number of parameters, GFLOPs, and inference latency. The experimental results indicate that in general, the transfer learning models have performed better than training the custom CNN, with the VGG16 model achieving the highest classification accuracy of 98.24%, the highest weighted F1-score of 98.24% and the highest macro-average AUC of 0.9997. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet50 exhibited similar predictive accuracy, with EfficientNet-B0 being a good tradeoff between computational complexity and classification accuracy and MobileNetV3 being a light-weight option for deployment on resource-limited systems. agriculture scenarios.Keywords—Sugarcane Leaf Disease, Deep Learning, Transfer Learning, Convolutional Neural Network, Precision Agriculture, Plant Disease Classification.INTRODUCTION Sugarcane is one of the most important commercial crops in the world and has a major contribution in sugar production, production of biofuels, and in the agriculture economy of many countries. It is however, highly susceptible to leaf diseases (Red Rot and Yellow Leaf Disease) which cause considerable economic losses and reduce the productivity of the crop and also affect the quality of the sugar. Thus early detection of disease is essential for timely action and successful crop management. Traditional disease diagnosis is mainly based on visual inspection by the agricultural experts. This is a common practice, but is time-consuming, subjective and not easily scalable to large plantations. Moreover, the fact that symptoms can be similar in the early stages of infection can lead to inconsistent diagnosis, delaying treatment and facilitating the spread of the disease, which has led to the development of automated disease detection systems based on computer vision and artificial intelligence. In recent years, the accuracy of plant disease classification has been greatly improved with the development of deep learning, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This has been further sped up by the use of transfer learning, which allows pretrained models to adapt to agricultural datasets with few annotated images. While these advances have been made, there remain a number of research challenges. Previous research typically focuses on a small number of architectures and mainly on the predictive accuracy, with computational efficiency and feasibility of deployment given relatively less attention. To overcome these shortcomings, the study compares and evaluates six architectures of deep learning for multiclass classification of sugarcane leaf diseases: Custom CNN, VGG16, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, and EfficientNet-B0. 3.1 Dataset and PreprocessingThe experiments were carried out using a publicly available dataset on Kaggle for sugarcane leaf disease with 1493 RGB images of three classes: Healthy (470), RedRot (518), and Yellow (505). The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test subsets using an approximately 70:15:15 split, resulting in 1044, 222, and 227 images respectively. The images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels and loaded with the TensorFlow's ImageDataGenerator. Data augmentation was only performed on the training set, such as random rotation, horizontal flipping, width shifting, height shifting, shear transformation and zooming, to enhance the generalization of the model. The images were not altered, as they were used to test the performance of the models on unseen images for both validation and testing. Since the input requirements varied across the different pre-trained architectures, different pre-processing functions were used for each architecture, while the custom CNN applied pixel-value normalization.Fig. 1. The custom CNN was trained from scratch for 40 epochs while the pretrained CNN architectures used a two-stage transfer learning approach. During the first phase, the convolutional backbone was frozen and only the newly added classifier was trained. The final backbone layers were then selectively unfrozen and fine-tuned in the second stage, with a lower learning rate to fine-tune the learned representations for the sugarcane disease classification. A custom convolutional neural network (CNN) and five ImageNet-pretrained transfer learning models-VGG16, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, and EfficientNet-B0 were trained and evaluated under the same experimental framework, using consistent data splitting and architecture-specific preprocessing where required.Experimental results showed that the transfer learning models generally performed better than the CNN trained from scratch. cific preprocessing where required.Experimental results showed that the transfer learning models generally performed better than the CNN trained from scratch. VGG16 demonstrated the best classification accuracy (98.24%), weighted F1 score (98.24%) and macro-average AUC (0.9997), showing strong discriminative performance for all three disease classes. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet50 also performed well in terms of classification accuracy, at 97.80% and 97.36%, respectively. In comparison, MobileNetV2 and MobileNetV3 had accuracies of 91.19% and 92.07%, respectively, and needed significantly fewer parameters and GFLOPs compared to the larger conventional architectures.The computational analysis also showed that the selection of the model is dependent on the deployment scenario that is intended. Custom CNN's single-image inference latency was the lowest measured at 2.203 ms, whereas MobileNetV2 and MobileNetV3 had latencies of 6.212 ms and 7.238 ms respectively. EfficientNet-B0 offered a good tradeoff between accuracy and computational complexity, with 97.80% accuracy, 4.84 million parameters and 0.39 GFLOPs per image. The results show that theoretical computational complexity is not always the same as runtime latency, and thus both should be taken into account when choosing a model for practical application.In general, the findings showed that the pretrained deep learning architectures have great potential in the field of automated sugarcane leaf disease classification and the need to choose an architecture based on the needs of the application. VGG16 is better for high classification accuracy, EfficientNet-B0 for a good balance of accuracy and complexity, and MobileNet for resource-limited applications.However, this study has a number of limitations. The experiments were performed with a single publicly available dataset that includes three disease classes, so the generalization to different real-world agricultural settings is yet to be proven.
